sections.h2: What speeds up a quick Edwardsville sale
sections.html:
Three things set the pace for a quick Edwardsville sale: how much work the house needs, whether the title is clean, and how fast the Madison County documents come together. A seller who has the parcel number, the payoff letter and any permit records in hand can move much sooner than one who starts collecting them after an offer arrives.

You can hire an agent and host showings, sell the home yourself, or take an as-is cash purchase that closes on the day you choose. The cash route skips repairs and open houses. Whichever you pick, the deed, transfer declaration and tax proration work the same way, and the sections below explain them.

  • Find the parcel number (PIN) printed on your Madison County tax bill.
  • Get a payoff letter from your lender and look for liens against the property.
  • Note whether anyone rents the home, since Edwardsville tracks rentals by registration.
  • Decide whether you want to close within weeks or can wait through a listing period.

Edwardsville is the Madison County seat, about 18 miles northeast of downtown St. Louis, with 26,463 residents. Southern Illinois University Edwardsville is based here, and the median age is a young 30.1. Most of the city lies in Edwardsville Community Unit School District 7, with small slivers in other districts, so check which district your own address falls in before writing a listing.

There are 9,828 households, and two thirds of them own their homes. The 2020 count listed 10,456 housing units with 14.2 percent of rental units vacant, so a landlord selling a house with a tenant should expect renters to have choices.

The $299,800 figure is a midpoint across the whole city. A Saint Louis Street classic, a newer subdivision house and a rental near campus can sit far apart, so set your asking price from recent closed sales of comparable houses on nearby streets.

Madison County has real storm exposure. The tornado outbreak of December 10 and 11, 2021 struck Edwardsville, where an EF3 tornado collapsed an Amazon warehouse. Lenders and insurers often ask about roof age, window condition and earlier storm repairs, so save receipts and permit records.

Temperatures swing widely, from the 19 degrees Fahrenheit of a typical January to 90 in July. The city sits in Climate Zone 4A under the International Energy Conservation Code, so heating and cooling equipment gets used hard. An old unit or a stained ceiling will show up on any inspection report.

Some owners skip the roof repair and sell to a buyer who accepts the damage.

sections.h2: Rental registration when an Edwardsville landlord sells
sections.html:
Edwardsville operates a Rental Registration and Inspection Program, and each rental must be registered annually. The form sets $40 for a single-family or mobile home building, $60 for a duplex and $25 per unit in buildings of three or more. Registrations received after January 31 pay a $75 late fee, a first re-inspection is free, and later ones cost $75.

The sale itself triggers paperwork. An ownership change requires deregistration, with Property Sold as one of the listed reasons, and a purchaser has 30 days from taking title to register. The city also refuses registration to any owner with unpaid fees or fines. Contact rentalregistration@cityofedwardsville.com or 618-307-1501 with questions.

  • File the deregistration once the sale closes so city records name the right owner.
  • Pay any fees or fines owed to the city before the closing date.
  • Tell the buyer which units have tenants, because inspections are requested before occupancy.
  • Smoke detectors are required in each sleeping room, within 15 feet of sleeping rooms and on every level, and carbon monoxide detectors within 15 feet of sleeping rooms.

The Madison County Recorder handles deeds for Edwardsville. The state charge is $.50 per $500 of taxable consideration, or part thereof, and the county charge is $.25 per $500, or part thereof. A PTAX declaration or a statement of exemption has to accompany the deed, and the exemptions sit in 35 ILCS 200/31-45.

The office has a few rules that catch do-it-yourself sellers. Every deed needs the buyer's name and mailing address for tax billing. A notarized Plat Act affidavit travels with it, and the permanent parcel number belongs on the document. If you pay by check, write the recording fee and the transfer tax on different checks. Ask the office for the current recording fee.

A closing agent can take over this paperwork, and you should read the transfer tax line on the settlement statement before signing.

The Treasurer bills real estate tax in four installments, due in July, September, October and December, on the 9th of each month. A late installment gains a 1.5 percent penalty for each 30 days it stays unpaid. Under 35 ILCS 200/20-15, a missing bill does not cancel the debt.

Illinois tax is paid after the year it covers, since taxes on one year's assessments are paid the next year. At closing, the settlement statement divides the bill, so ask for that split in writing. If taxes go unpaid they are sold at the annual tax sale, and redemption can run two to three years. A lien of that kind complicates any sale, so clear it first.

Assessment appeals go to the Madison County Board of Review, which accepts filings up to 30 days after assessments are published. Relief is available for general homestead, senior homestead, disabled persons and senior freeze. Phone the Chief County Assessment Office to learn which apply to your parcel.

Before closing, ask the Treasurer's office for a paid-to-date printout so the title company can confirm which installments are settled.

sections.h2: Permit records before selling in Edwardsville
sections.html:
Buyers and their lenders ask about work done to the house. Edwardsville's building permit application covers new construction, remodels, garages, roofs, and electrical, plumbing and mechanical work, and it includes a line asking whether the property is a rental. The roofing section asks for an Illinois roofing license number.

An open permit or an unpermitted addition can stall a closing. Collect records for decks, finished basements, water heaters and furnaces before you list. Ask the city whether anything on your address remains open, and finish it before you sign a purchase contract.

faqs.q: What if tenants live in my Edwardsville house?
faqs.a: A sale is still possible. The city requires owners to register rentals each year and to deregister when the property sells, so file the Property Sold deregistration after closing. The buyer registers within 30 days of taking ownership.

faqs.q: How much transfer tax will an Edwardsville seller see on the settlement statement?
faqs.a: The state charges $.50 per $500 and Madison County $.25 per $500, each on taxable consideration or part thereof. Your closing agent turns that into dollars for the statement.

faqs.q: Who records the deed on an Edwardsville home?
faqs.a: The Madison County Recorder. The deed arrives with a PTAX declaration or exemption statement, a notarized Plat Act affidavit, the parcel number and the buyer's tax billing address. Title companies usually submit the package.

faqs.q: How many times a year does Madison County bill property tax?
faqs.a: Four times, from July through December, with a 1.5 percent monthly penalty on late installments. The Treasurer's website shows what has been paid on your parcel.

faqs.q: Will a cash sale close faster than a listing in Edwardsville?
faqs.a: Often yes, since there is no marketing period, mortgage approval or repair haggling. County paperwork, payoff and title review still apply, so a clean title sets the real pace.
